questions.q: Why is this capstone explicitly not a replay of the Northbridge Retail checkout incident?
options: Because Northbridge's incident was fictional and can't be reused
Because the capstone is meant to demonstrate the student's own original build, applying everything learned to a service of their own choosing
Because the course ran out of material about Northbridge
Because grading tools can't evaluate a repeated scenario
questions.explain: Northbridge was the running example used to teach concepts. The capstone is meant to be the student's own portfolio piece, demonstrating they can apply the material independently.

questions.q: What size of service is recommended for this capstone?
options: A large multi-service distributed system, to maximize complexity
Something so trivial it has no real failure modes, since it's easier to finish
One real, running service with a couple of operations and roughly one dependency — small enough to finish, real enough to be worth showing
A purely theoretical service with no code at all
questions.explain: The lesson recommends a right-sized service: not trivial (nothing interesting to observe) and not so large it consumes the whole capstone on building the service rather than instrumenting it.

questions.q: What should be decided in writing before any instrumentation code is written?
options: The company's annual budget
The service's golden signals, what tools will be used to instrument it, where the data will live and be visualized, and 2-3 planned alerts
The exact wording of the final presentation slides
Nothing — instrumentation should always be improvised as you go
questions.explain: The lesson calls for planning four things up front: golden signals, instrumentation tools, where data lives/is visualized, and draft alert conditions — before writing any code.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what kind of alerts should be planned for the capstone service?
options: As many threshold alerts as possible, covering every available metric
Symptom-based, actionable alerts, consistent with the alert-fatigue lesson earlier in the chapter
Only alerts that page someone every time any metric changes
No alerts — alerting is out of scope for the capstone
questions.explain: The plan explicitly calls for 2-3 alerts that are symptom-based and actionable, applying the alert-fatigue principles from Lesson 28 rather than arbitrary threshold alerts.

questions.q: What are the expected deliverables by the end of the capstone (Lesson 31)?
options: A written exam only, no running code
A running instrumented service, a dashboard with several meaningful panels, 2-3 real alert rules, and a write-up of design decisions
A single screenshot of a dashboard with no supporting service
A list of every monitoring tool that exists, with no implementation
questions.explain: The lesson lists concrete deliverables: a running service with metrics/logs/tracing, a dashboard with 4-6 meaningful panels, 2-3 real alert rules, and a short design write-up for a portfolio.
